chem_edx.5.0.summary: Most metals in the periodic table are **transition metals**, found in the central block between groups 2 and 3. Compared with group 1 metals they have **high melting points**, **high densities**, form **coloured compounds** and, as metals or compounds, show **catalytic activity**. Iron is the spec's example: it melts at about 1538 °C, is dense, forms green iron(II) and orange-brown iron(III) compounds, and is the **catalyst in the Haber process** for making ammonia.

core.p: The transition metals sit in the **central block** of the periodic table, between group 2 and group 3. Because this block is so wide, **most metals are transition metals**. You do not need to learn every one, but you must know their typical properties and be able to use **iron** as the example.
bullets: Found in the **central block**, between groups 2 and 3, starting in period 4.
Common examples: **iron (Fe)**, copper (Cu), nickel (Ni), chromium (Cr), zinc (Zn), manganese (Mn), titanium (Ti), gold (Au), silver (Ag), platinum (Pt).
They are **not numbered as a group** in the GCSE table; they are just called the transition metals.
**Most metals are transition metals**, so 'typical metal' properties in industry often means transition metal properties.
They are much **less reactive** than group 1 metals: iron does not react violently with water like sodium does.

callouts.p: Recall that most metals are transition metals and that their typical properties include high melting point, high density, the formation of coloured compounds and catalytic activity of the metals and their compounds, as exemplified by iron.

core.p: Edexcel names four typical properties of transition metals. Learn them as a list of four, because 'state two typical properties' style questions are very common and each correct property scores a mark.
bullets: **High melting point** (iron about 1538 °C).
**High density** (iron about 7.9 g/cm3, so a small block feels heavy).
**Form coloured compounds** (iron(II) compounds are green, iron(III) compounds are orange-brown).
**Catalytic activity** of the metals and their compounds (iron is the catalyst in the Haber process).
They also have all the **general metal properties**: good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable, ductile, shiny when freshly cut.
They are typically **hard and strong**, which is why they are used as structural metals.

callouts.p: Write 'high melting point', 'high density', 'form coloured compounds' and 'act as catalysts'. Vague answers such as 'strong' or 'heavy' often do not score.

core.p: Transition metals have **giant metallic structures**: a lattice of **positive metal ions** surrounded by a sea of **delocalised electrons**. The **strong electrostatic attraction** between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons holds the structure together. A lot of energy is needed to overcome these strong forces, so the melting point is high.
bullets: Metallic bonding = **electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons**.
Transition metals have **strong metallic bonding**, much stronger than in group 1 metals.
Melting means overcoming the attraction throughout the whole giant lattice, so **lots of energy** is needed.
Iron melts at about **1538 °C**; sodium melts at only about **98 °C**.
High melting point is why iron, steel and titanium can be used for engines, furnaces and structural frames that get hot.

callouts.p: Metals are giant structures. Never say 'weak intermolecular forces' or 'covalent bonds' when explaining metal melting points. Say strong attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons.

core.p: Density = mass / volume. Transition metal atoms have a **large mass** for their size and are **closely packed** in the lattice, so a given volume contains a lot of mass. Group 1 atoms are lighter and larger, so group 1 metals have low densities (lithium, sodium and potassium even float on water).
bullets: Density = **mass / volume** (units g/cm3 or kg/m3).
Iron has a density of about **7.9 g/cm3**, nearly eight times that of water.
Sodium has a density of about **0.97 g/cm3**, so it floats on water.
High density is useful where weight helps (anchors, counterweights) but a disadvantage in aircraft, which is why lower density metals such as aluminium or titanium alloys are chosen there.
Compare data: if a metal in a table has density above about 4 g/cm3 and a high melting point, it is likely to be a transition metal.

callouts.p: Exams often give a table of melting points and densities and ask which metal is a transition metal. Pick the one with the highest values AND say 'because it has a high melting point and high density', quoting the numbers.

core.p: A big difference from group 1 and group 2: transition metal **compounds are coloured**, both as solids and in solution. Group 1 compounds such as sodium chloride are white solids that give colourless solutions. The colour comes from the transition metal ion, and the **same metal can give different colours** depending on the charge on its ion.
bullets: **Iron(II) compounds** (Fe2+), e.g. iron(II) sulfate, are **pale green**.
**Iron(III) compounds** (Fe3+), e.g. iron(III) chloride, are **orange-brown / yellow-brown**.
**Copper(II) compounds** (Cu2+), e.g. copper(II) sulfate solution, are **blue**.
Coloured compounds are used as **pigments** in paints, glazes and stained glass.
Note the metal itself is usually grey or silvery (copper and gold are exceptions); it is the **compounds** that are coloured.
Zinc compounds are white, so not every compound in the central block is coloured; for exams stick to iron and copper as examples.

callouts.p: Iron forms ions with two different charges, Fe2+ and Fe3+. Iron(II) compounds are green; iron(III) compounds are orange-brown. The Roman numeral in the name gives the charge on the ion.

core.p: Group 1 metals always form 1+ ions and group 2 metals always form 2+ ions. Transition metals can often form **ions with different charges**. Iron forms **Fe2+** and **Fe3+**, which is why iron has two oxides, two chlorides and two sets of colours. This links to rusting (5.2C) where iron is oxidised to iron(III).
bullets: Iron(II) = Fe2+, e.g. FeSO4 iron(II) sulfate, FeCl2 iron(II) chloride, FeO iron(II) oxide.
Iron(III) = Fe3+, e.g. FeCl3 iron(III) chloride, Fe2O3 iron(III) oxide (the main part of rust and of the ore haematite).
Formula check: Fe3+ with O2- needs 2 x (3+) = 6+ and 3 x (2-) = 6-, so **Fe2O3**.
Copper forms Cu2+ (copper(II)) in most GCSE compounds, e.g. CuO, CuSO4.
Fe2+ can be **oxidised** to Fe3+ (loss of an electron): Fe2+ → Fe3+ + e-. Green iron(II) solutions slowly go orange-brown in air for this reason.

callouts.p: The Roman numeral in a name such as iron(III) chloride shows the charge on the metal ion: iron(III) contains Fe3+ ions.

core.p: Transition metals and their compounds are often good **catalysts**. A catalyst **speeds up a reaction without being used up**, by providing an **alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy**. Because it is not used up, a small amount can be used again and again, which saves money and energy in industry.
bullets: Catalyst: increases the **rate** of a reaction, is **not used up** (chemically unchanged at the end), and is not part of the overall equation.
It works by providing an **alternative pathway with lower activation energy**, so more collisions have enough energy to react.
Both the **metals** and their **compounds** can be catalysts (spec wording).
A catalyst does **not** change the yield at equilibrium or the energy change of the reaction; it only makes equilibrium reached faster.
Catalysts are often used as **powders, pellets or fine gauze** to give a large surface area.

callouts.p: A substance that speeds up the rate of a reaction without being altered in mass or chemical composition at the end of the reaction; it provides an alternative pathway of lower activation energy.

core.h: Iron: catalyst in the Haber process
core.p: The spec uses **iron** as the example of a transition metal catalyst. In the **Haber process** nitrogen and hydrogen react to make ammonia. The reaction is slow because breaking the strong triple bond in nitrogen needs a lot of energy. An **iron catalyst** lowers the activation energy so ammonia forms quickly enough to be economic, at a lower temperature than would otherwise be needed.
bullets: Equation: **N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g)** (reversible; forward reaction exothermic).
Conditions (detail in 5.19C-5.21C): about **450 °C**, about **200 atmospheres**, **iron catalyst**.
The iron is used as small lumps/pellets to give a **large surface area**.
Without the catalyst the reaction would be far too slow at 450 °C; a higher temperature would speed it up but **lower the equilibrium yield** of ammonia, so the catalyst is essential.
Ammonia is used to make **fertilisers** (e.g. ammonium nitrate), so the iron catalyst helps feed the world.
The iron is not used up, so it lasts for years in the reactor.

callouts.p: Iron = catalyst in the Haber process for making ammonia. This is the example Edexcel mark schemes expect for 'catalytic activity of transition metals'.

core.p: Iron is the one the spec names, but knowing other examples helps in 'suggest' and 6 mark questions and shows that catalytic activity really is a typical property of the whole block.
bullets: **Nickel**: catalyst for adding hydrogen to vegetable oils (hydrogenation) to make spreads.
**Vanadium(V) oxide**, V2O5: catalyst in the Contact process for making sulfuric acid (a transition metal **compound**).
**Platinum, palladium, rhodium**: catalysts in car **catalytic converters**, removing carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides.
**Manganese(IV) oxide**, MnO2: catalyst for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
Copper compounds catalyse some reactions too, e.g. copper(II) sulfate speeds up the reaction of zinc with dilute acid.

callouts.p: If asked to show that transition metal compounds are catalysts, MnO2 or V2O5 are good examples; for the metal itself use iron in the Haber process.

core.p: Put everything for iron together so you can answer any 'using iron as an example' question in one go.
bullets: Symbol **Fe**, a transition metal in period 4.
Melting point about **1538 °C**: high.
Density about **7.9 g/cm3**: high.
Forms **Fe2+** (green compounds) and **Fe3+** (orange-brown compounds).
**Catalyst in the Haber process**: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3.
Hard and strong, good conductor, magnetic; mostly used as **steel** (an alloy of iron with carbon, see 5.5C-5.7C).
Corrodes (rusts) in the presence of **both water and oxygen** (see 5.2C).

core.p: Many questions ask you to **compare** transition metals with the alkali metals. Use comparative words (higher, lower, more, less) and give both sides of the comparison.
bullets: Transition metals have **higher melting points** than group 1 metals.
Transition metals have **higher densities** than group 1 metals.
Transition metals are **harder and stronger**; group 1 metals are soft.
Transition metal compounds are **coloured**; group 1 compounds are **white** and dissolve to give colourless solutions.
Transition metals are **much less reactive** with water and oxygen.
Transition metals and their compounds are used as **catalysts**; group 1 metals are not.
Transition metals form **ions with different charges**; group 1 metals only form 1+ ions.

callouts.p: 'Iron has a high melting point' is a statement. 'Iron has a higher melting point than sodium' is a comparison. When the question says compare, use the comparison form.

core.p: Exam questions often ask why a transition metal is chosen for a job. Link one property to the use and explain why it matters.
bullets: **Iron/steel girders and car bodies**: strong and hard; high melting point means they do not soften in normal heat.
**Copper pipes and wires**: good conductor, malleable/ductile, does not react with water.
**Cobalt and copper compounds in glass and ceramic glazes**: they are **coloured**.
**Iron in ammonia plants**: **catalyst**, speeds up the reaction, not used up.
**Tungsten** filament lamps: extremely high melting point (about 3400 °C), so it can glow white-hot without melting.
**Titanium** in jet engines: high melting point and strong, but lower density than iron.

core.p: This point is usually tested with short recall (1 to 2 marks), data interpretation (choose the transition metal from a table) or a longer compare/explain question. Plan the four properties first, then add evidence and reasons.
bullets: **State** questions: just name the property, e.g. 'forms coloured compounds'.
**Explain** questions: give the property and the reason, e.g. high melting point because of strong attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons.
**Data** questions: quote numbers with units from the table.
For catalysts, always say **speeds up the reaction** and **is not used up**; for top marks add **lower activation energy**.
Do not mix up **iron(II)** green and **iron(III)** orange-brown.

callouts.p: Think 'Many Dense Colourful Catalysts': Melting point high, Density high, Coloured compounds, Catalysts.

analogy.p: Think of group 1 metals as flimsy party balloons and transition metals as steel toolboxes. The toolbox is heavy (high density), survives a bonfire (high melting point), comes in coloured paint jobs depending on the model (iron(II) green, iron(III) orange-brown) and contains a tool that helps others do their jobs faster without being used up itself (catalyst). Where it breaks down: the colours belong to the compounds, not the metal itself, and a catalyst does take part in the reaction temporarily, unlike a tool that only watches.

terms.d: A metal in the central block of the periodic table, between group 2 and group 3.
The wide section of the periodic table between groups 2 and 3 where the transition metals are found.
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid; high for transition metals.
Mass per unit volume (density = mass / volume), measured in g/cm3 or kg/m3.
The electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons.
Outer electrons that are free to move through the whole metal structure.
A compound of a transition metal that absorbs some visible light, so it appears coloured, e.g. green iron(II) sulfate.
Fe2+, an iron ion with a 2+ charge; its compounds are pale green.
Fe3+, an iron ion with a 3+ charge; its compounds are orange-brown.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up, by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.
The minimum energy that particles must have when they collide for a reaction to happen.
The industrial process that makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen, N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, using an iron catalyst.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions react, e.g. green Fe(OH)2 when sodium hydroxide is added to Fe2+ ions.
A group 1 metal; soft, low density, low melting point, very reactive, forms white compounds.
Loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen), e.g. Fe2+ → Fe3+ + e-.

mistakes.w: Transition metals are in group 2.
mistakes.r: Transition metals are in the central block between groups 2 and 3.

mistakes.w: Transition metals are coloured.
mistakes.r: Transition metals form coloured compounds; the metals themselves are mostly grey/silver.

mistakes.w: Iron(II) compounds are orange-brown and iron(III) are green.
mistakes.r: Iron(II) (Fe2+) compounds are green; iron(III) (Fe3+) compounds are orange-brown.

mistakes.w: A catalyst is used up / gets used in the reaction.
mistakes.r: A catalyst speeds up the reaction and is not used up; it is chemically unchanged at the end.

mistakes.w: A catalyst gives the particles more energy.
mistakes.r: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.

mistakes.w: Iron is the catalyst in the Contact process.
mistakes.r: Iron is the catalyst in the Haber process for ammonia (vanadium(V) oxide is used in the Contact process).

mistakes.w: Metals have high melting points because of strong covalent bonds / intermolecular forces.
mistakes.r: Strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons needs lots of energy to overcome.

mistakes.w: Transition metals are heavy.
mistakes.r: Transition metals have a high density (large mass per unit volume).

mistakes.w: Transition metals are more reactive than group 1 metals.
mistakes.r: Transition metals are much less reactive than group 1 metals.

exam.q: State where the transition metals are found in the periodic table.
model: In the central block, between group 2 and group 3.
exam.tip: 'Middle' is accepted by some mark schemes but 'between groups 2 and 3' is safest.

exam.q: Give two typical properties of transition metals, other than being good conductors of electricity.
model: High melting point / high density.
Form coloured compounds / act as catalysts.
exam.tip: Any two of the four spec properties score; do not give general metal properties.

exam.q: Iron is used as a catalyst in the Haber process. Name the product of the Haber process.
model: Ammonia (NH3).
exam.tip: Learn the pairing iron and Haber process.

exam.q: Explain how the iron catalyst increases the rate of the Haber process.
model: Provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
So a greater proportion of collisions have enough energy to react / more successful collisions per second.
exam.tip: Do not say the catalyst gives particles more energy.

exam.q: A student adds sodium hydroxide solution to iron(II) sulfate solution and to iron(III) chloride solution. Describe what they would see in each case.
model: Iron(II): green precipitate.
Iron(III): orange-brown precipitate.
exam.tip: Say 'precipitate', not just a colour.

exam.q: Metal X has a melting point of 1455 °C and a density of 8.9 g/cm3. Metal Y has a melting point of 64 °C and a density of 0.86 g/cm3. Which metal is a transition metal? Give two reasons.
model: Metal X.
It has a high melting point (1455 °C).
It has a high density (8.9 g/cm3).
exam.tip: Quote the data to justify each reason.

exam.q: Explain why iron has a high melting point.
model: Iron has a giant metallic structure / metallic bonding.
Strong electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons.
A lot of energy is needed to overcome these forces.
exam.tip: Three linked ideas: structure, force, energy.

exam.q: Iron forms two chlorides, FeCl2 and FeCl3. Name these two compounds and give the colour of each.
model: FeCl2 is iron(II) chloride, green.
FeCl3 is iron(III) chloride, orange-brown / yellow-brown.
exam.tip: The Roman numeral equals the charge on the iron ion.

exam.q: Suggest why using a catalyst in the Haber process saves money.
model: Reaction is fast enough at a lower temperature, so less energy / fuel is needed.
Catalyst is not used up so it does not need replacing often.
exam.tip: Two separate economic reasons.

exam.q: Compare the properties of iron with those of sodium. Refer to physical properties, compounds and uses as catalysts.
model: Iron has a much higher melting point than sodium (about 1538 °C compared to 98 °C).
Iron has a higher density than sodium; sodium floats on water.
Iron is hard and strong; sodium is soft and can be cut with a knife.
Iron compounds are coloured (green iron(II), orange-brown iron(III)); sodium compounds are white / give colourless solutions.
Iron is a catalyst in the Haber process; sodium is not used as a catalyst.
Iron is much less reactive than sodium; sodium reacts vigorously with water, iron only rusts slowly.
Iron forms ions with different charges (Fe2+ and Fe3+); sodium only forms Na+.
exam.tip: Every point should mention both metals, using comparative words.

exam.q: Iron(III) oxide is found in rust. Write its formula, given the ions Fe3+ and O2-.
model: Fe2O3.
exam.tip: Balance the charges: 2 x 3+ = 6+, 3 x 2- = 6-.

worked.q: Use the table to identify which metal is a transition metal and explain your choice. Metal A: mp 98 °C, density 0.97 g/cm3, white chloride. Metal B: mp 1538 °C, density 7.87 g/cm3, green and orange-brown chlorides. Metal C: mp 660 °C, density 2.70 g/cm3, white chloride.
steps: Look for high melting point: B (1538 °C) is far higher than A (98 °C) and C (660 °C).
Look for high density: B (7.87 g/cm3) is highest.
Look for coloured compounds: only B forms coloured chlorides (green and orange-brown).
Two colours of chloride means two ions with different charges, Fe2+ and Fe3+, which suggests iron.
Conclude with reasons linked to the data.
worked.ans: Metal B is the transition metal (iron) because it has the highest melting point (1538 °C), the highest density (7.87 g/cm3) and forms coloured compounds.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why iron is used in the Haber process and what difference it makes.
steps: State the role: iron is a catalyst.
Give the equation: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3.
Explain the mechanism: it provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful and the rate increases.
State it is not used up, so it can be reused for a long time.
Link to conditions: a reasonable rate is achieved at about 450 °C, so a very high temperature (which would lower the yield of the exothermic forward reaction and cost more energy) is not needed.
Note it does not change the equilibrium yield, only how quickly equilibrium is reached.
worked.ans: Iron is a transition metal catalyst that lowers the activation energy, making ammonia form quickly at a compromise temperature, without being used up and without changing the yield.

worked.q: A metal oxide of a transition metal contains Fe3+ ions. Work out the formula and predict the colour of the solid.
steps: Fe3+ has charge 3+; oxide ion O2- has charge 2-.
Lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6.
Need 2 Fe3+ (6+) and 3 O2- (6-).
Formula Fe2O3, iron(III) oxide.
Iron(III) compounds are orange-brown / red-brown.
worked.ans: Fe2O3, iron(III) oxide, which is a red-brown / orange-brown solid (as in rust).

chem_edx.5.1.summary: **Corrosion** is the **oxidation** of a metal by substances around it, and **rusting** is the corrosion of iron and steel, which needs **both oxygen and water**. Rusting is prevented by **excluding oxygen and/or water** (painting, oiling, greasing, plastic coating, tin plating) or by **sacrificial protection**, where a **more reactive metal** such as zinc or magnesium is oxidised instead of the iron. **Electroplating** uses electrolysis to coat an object (the **cathode**) with a thin layer of another metal, to improve its **appearance** and/or its **resistance to corrosion**.

core.p: Most metals react slowly with substances in their surroundings, especially **oxygen** and **water**. This gradual destruction of a metal is called **corrosion**. Because the metal gains oxygen and its atoms lose electrons to form positive ions, corrosion is an **oxidation** reaction. The more reactive the metal, the more easily it corrodes.
bullets: Corrosion = **oxidation of a metal** by reaction with substances in the environment (usually oxygen, often with water).
Oxidation can be described as **gain of oxygen** or **loss of electrons**.
**Rusting is a specific type of corrosion**: the corrosion of **iron** (and steel, which is mainly iron).
Only iron and steel 'rust'; other metals 'corrode' (e.g. copper turns green, silver tarnishes black).
Corrosion weakens structures (bridges, cars, ships), so preventing it saves a lot of money and keeps people safe.

callouts.p: Corrosion is the oxidation of metals. Rusting is a specific example of corrosion, of iron, which requires both water and oxygen.

core.p: Iron rusts only when **both oxygen (from air) and water** are present. The product, **rust**, is **hydrated iron(III) oxide**. Rust is crumbly and **flakes off**, exposing fresh iron underneath, so rusting carries on until the iron is eaten away. This is different from aluminium, whose oxide layer protects it.
bullets: Word equation: **iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide**.
Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, written Fe2O3.xH2O (x = a variable number of water molecules).
A simple symbol equation for the oxide part: 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3.
**Both** oxygen and water are needed: no oxygen = no rust; no water = no rust.
**Salt** (e.g. sea water or road salt in winter) **speeds up** rusting, but is not required.
Rust flakes off, so it does **not** protect the iron below; rusting continues.

callouts.p: Rusting requires BOTH water AND oxygen. Removing either one stops rusting. This idea is behind every barrier method.
Saying 'iron rusts in air' loses the mark. Say iron rusts when it is in contact with both oxygen and water.

core.p: A classic experiment uses three iron nails in test tubes, each missing a different condition. Only the nail with both air and water rusts. Leave the tubes for about a week and compare.
bullets: **Tube A**: nail in tap water, open to air. Has oxygen and water, so it **rusts**.
**Tube B**: nail in **boiled water** with a **layer of oil** on top and a bung. Boiling removes dissolved oxygen; oil stops oxygen dissolving back in. **No rust**, so oxygen is needed.
**Tube C**: nail in air dried by **anhydrous calcium chloride**, with a bung. No water vapour. **No rust**, so water is needed.
**Control variables**: same type and size of nail, same temperature, same time, nails cleaned with sandpaper first.
Conclusion: iron needs **both oxygen and water** to rust.

callouts.p: A common 2 mark question: boiling removes dissolved oxygen (air); the oil layer stops air/oxygen dissolving back into the water.

core.p: For grade 9 you should describe rusting as **oxidation** in terms of electrons. Iron atoms **lose electrons** to become iron ions. Oxygen (with water) **gains** those electrons, so oxygen is reduced. Since oxidation and reduction happen together, rusting is a **redox** reaction.
bullets: Iron is oxidised: **Fe → Fe2+ + 2e-**, and then further to Fe3+ (Fe2+ → Fe3+ + e-).
Overall the iron ends up as Fe3+ in hydrated iron(III) oxide.
**OIL RIG**: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain.
Oxygen gains electrons, so it is **reduced**.
Any method that stops iron losing electrons, or stops oxygen and water reaching it, prevents rusting.

callouts.p: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or the loss of electrons.

core.h: Why aluminium does not keep corroding
core.p: Aluminium is **more reactive** than iron, yet aluminium objects last for years. This is because aluminium reacts with oxygen to form a thin, tough layer of **aluminium oxide** that **sticks to the surface** and stops oxygen and water reaching the metal underneath. Rust, in contrast, flakes off.
bullets: Aluminium oxide layer is **thin, unreactive and does not flake off**: a natural barrier.
Rust is **porous and flaky**, so it does not protect the iron.
This is why aluminium is used for window frames, drinks cans and aircraft without needing paint.
Exam trap: aluminium's resistance is **not** because it is unreactive; it is because of its protective oxide layer.

callouts.p: Aluminium is above iron in the reactivity series. It resists corrosion only because of the protective oxide layer.

core.h: Preventing rusting by excluding oxygen and water
core.p: Since rusting needs **both oxygen and water**, coating iron with a **barrier** stops them reaching the surface. These methods work only while the barrier is **unbroken**: once scratched or chipped, oxygen and water reach the iron and it rusts.
bullets: **Painting**: car bodies, bridges, railings. Cheap for large structures; must be repainted if chipped.
**Oiling or greasing**: bike chains, gears, tools, machinery with moving parts (paint would rub off). Needs reapplying; messy.
**Plastic coating**: garden chairs, wire fences, dish racks, coat hangers. Tough and waterproof.
**Tin plating**: food cans ('tin cans' are steel coated in tin). Tin is unreactive and non-toxic.
**Storing with a drying agent** or in dry conditions removes water (e.g. silica gel packets with tools).
All of these keep oxygen and/or water away from the iron surface.

callouts.p: Painting, oiling, greasing, plastic coating and tin plating all prevent rusting by excluding oxygen and water from the iron.

core.p: In **sacrificial protection**, iron is attached to or coated with a **more reactive metal**, such as **zinc** or **magnesium**. The more reactive metal **loses electrons more readily**, so it is **oxidised instead of the iron**. The reactive metal is 'sacrificed': it corrodes away while the iron is protected. This works **even if the iron is exposed** to oxygen and water.
bullets: The protecting metal must be **more reactive than iron** (higher in the reactivity series): magnesium or zinc.
It is **oxidised in preference** to iron: Zn → Zn2+ + 2e- or Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-.
Electrons flow from the more reactive metal to the iron, so iron does not lose electrons and is **not oxidised**.
**Blocks of magnesium or zinc** are bolted to **ship hulls**, oil rigs and buried steel **pipelines**.
The blocks corrode away and must be **replaced** regularly, which is cheaper than replacing the ship or pipe.
Copper or tin cannot be used: they are **less reactive** than iron.

callouts.p: Protecting iron by attaching a more reactive metal, which is oxidised (corrodes) instead of the iron.

core.p: **Galvanising** means coating iron or steel with a layer of **zinc** (often by dipping into molten zinc). It protects in **two ways**: the zinc is a **barrier** that keeps out oxygen and water, and if the coating is scratched the zinc gives **sacrificial protection** because it is more reactive than iron. So galvanised iron does not rust even when damaged.
bullets: Zinc coating excludes oxygen and water (**barrier**).
If scratched, zinc is **oxidised in preference** to the exposed iron (**sacrificial**): Zn → Zn2+ + 2e-.
Zinc also forms a fairly protective layer of zinc compounds on its surface.
Uses: **steel buckets, dustbins, corrugated roofing, nails, lamp posts, car bodies, crash barriers**.
Galvanising is not usually used for food cans because zinc compounds can be harmful in acidic foods.

callouts.p: For 'explain why galvanised iron does not rust when scratched': zinc is more reactive than iron (1), so zinc is oxidised / loses electrons instead of iron (1).

core.p: Tin and zinc coatings look similar but behave very differently once scratched. **Tin is less reactive than iron**, so it can only act as a **barrier**. If a tin can is scratched, the exposed iron is more reactive than the tin, so the **iron is oxidised** and actually rusts **faster** than uncoated iron would.
bullets: Tin plating: good while intact, **non-toxic and unreactive**, ideal for **food cans**.
Scratched tin plate: **iron corrodes**, faster than normal, because iron is more reactive than tin.
Galvanised (zinc) coating: **zinc corrodes instead** when scratched, iron stays protected.
So: dented or scratched food cans can rust badly; galvanised buckets do not.
Choosing a method depends on use: food contact (tin), outdoor toughness (zinc), moving parts (oil).

callouts.p: Tin does NOT give sacrificial protection. Only a metal MORE reactive than iron (zinc, magnesium) is sacrificial.

core.p: **Electroplating** uses **electrolysis** to coat a metal object with a thin layer of another metal. It is used to **improve appearance** (e.g. a shiny silver, gold or chromium finish) and/or to **improve resistance to corrosion** (the plating metal is less reactive or forms a barrier that keeps out oxygen and water). A thin plate is much **cheaper** than making the whole object from the expensive metal.
bullets: **Silver plating** of cutlery and trophies: attractive and resists corrosion; cheaper than solid silver.
**Gold plating** of jewellery and electrical connectors: attractive, does not tarnish, good conductor.
**Chromium plating** of taps, car bumpers and bike handlebars: very shiny, hard and corrosion resistant.
**Nickel plating**: corrosion resistance, often used under chromium.
**Tin plating** of steel for food cans: corrosion resistant and non-toxic.
**Copper plating**: often used as a base layer or on electronics.

callouts.p: Electroplating improves the appearance and/or the resistance to corrosion of metal objects.

core.p: The object to be plated is made the **cathode** (negative electrode). The **anode** (positive electrode) is a piece of the **plating metal**. The **electrolyte** is a solution containing **ions of the plating metal**. When the current flows, metal ions are attracted to the cathode, gain electrons and are deposited as a thin layer of metal on the object. At the anode, the plating metal atoms lose electrons and dissolve as ions, keeping the concentration of ions in the electrolyte constant.
bullets: **Object = cathode (-)**: positive metal ions are attracted and **reduced**, e.g. **Ag+ + e- → Ag**.
**Plating metal = anode (+)**: atoms are **oxidised** and go into solution, e.g. **Ag → Ag+ + e-**.
**Electrolyte**: contains ions of the plating metal, e.g. **silver nitrate** solution for silver; **copper(II) sulfate** for copper (Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu).
The anode gets **thinner**; the object (cathode) gets **heavier** by the same mass of metal.
Thickness of plating increases with **larger current** and **longer time**.
Object must be **clean** (grease-free) so the plating sticks evenly.

callouts.p: Positive is Anode, Negative Is Cathode. The object being plated always goes on the negative cathode, because metal ions are positive and are attracted to it.

core.p: Exam questions often describe an object and ask you to suggest and justify a method. Match the method to how the object is used.
bullets: **Moving parts** (chains, hinges, gears): oil or grease; paint would rub off and oil also lubricates.
**Food containers**: tin plating; tin is unreactive and non-toxic.
**Ships, pipelines, oil rigs**: sacrificial blocks of magnesium or zinc; too large or underwater to repaint easily.
**Outdoor steel likely to be scratched** (roofs, buckets, crash barriers): galvanising; protected even when scratched.
**Decorative items** (cutlery, jewellery, taps): electroplating with silver, gold or chromium for appearance and corrosion resistance.
**Large structures** (bridges, railings): paint; cheap and easy to apply over a large area.

core.p: This point is tested with recall of conditions, explaining prevention methods using reactivity and electrons, interpreting the rusting experiment, and describing electroplating. Always name the electrode and the electrolyte when describing electroplating.
bullets: Rusting conditions: say **oxygen AND water**.
Barrier methods: say they **exclude (keep out) oxygen and water**.
Sacrificial protection: say **more reactive metal**, **oxidised / loses electrons instead of iron**.
Electroplating: **object = cathode**, **plating metal = anode**, **electrolyte contains ions of plating metal**.
Higher tier: half equations at each electrode, e.g. Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu at the cathode.

callouts.p: Mark schemes want 'oxygen' (not just 'air') and 'water' (or 'moisture').

analogy.p: Barrier methods are like a raincoat: as long as it has no holes, the rain (water and oxygen) cannot reach you, but one tear and you get wet. Sacrificial protection is like a bodyguard who steps in front of you and takes the hit: zinc or magnesium gets 'attacked' (oxidised) instead of the iron, even if the iron is exposed. Galvanising is a bodyguard wearing a raincoat over you. Where it breaks down: a bodyguard chooses to step in, but zinc is oxidised first simply because it loses electrons more easily, and it is eventually used up completely.

exam.q: Name the two substances that must be present for iron to rust.
model: Oxygen (from air).
Water.
exam.tip: 'Air' alone does not score; say oxygen.

exam.q: Define the term corrosion.
model: The oxidation of a metal (by reaction with substances in the environment such as oxygen/water).
exam.tip: Key word: oxidation.

exam.q: In a rusting experiment, a nail is placed in boiled water with a layer of oil on top. Explain why the water is boiled and why oil is added.
model: Boiling removes dissolved oxygen / air.
Oil stops oxygen / air dissolving back into the water.
exam.tip: Two separate reasons, one per mark.

exam.q: Explain how painting prevents the rusting of a steel bridge.
model: Paint forms a barrier.
Which excludes / keeps out oxygen and water from the iron.
exam.tip: Name both oxygen and water.

exam.q: Explain why a bicycle chain is oiled rather than painted.
model: Oil excludes oxygen and water, preventing rusting.
Paint would rub off moving parts / oil also lubricates.
exam.tip: Link the choice to the moving parts.

exam.q: Blocks of magnesium are attached to the steel hull of a ship. Explain how this prevents the hull from rusting.
model: Magnesium is more reactive than iron.
Magnesium loses electrons / is oxidised in preference to iron.
So iron is not oxidised; this is sacrificial protection.
exam.tip: Use 'more reactive' and 'oxidised instead of'.

exam.q: Explain why galvanised iron does not rust even when scratched, but tin-plated iron does rust when scratched.
model: Zinc is more reactive than iron.
So zinc is oxidised / corrodes instead of iron (sacrificial protection).
Tin is less reactive than iron.
So when scratched, the exposed iron is oxidised / tin acts only as a barrier.
exam.tip: Compare both coatings with iron's reactivity.

exam.q: A student wants to copper plate an iron key. State what should be used as the anode, the cathode and the electrolyte.
model: Anode: copper.
Cathode: the iron key.
Electrolyte: copper(II) sulfate solution (a solution containing Cu2+ ions).
exam.tip: The object always goes on the cathode.

exam.q: Write the half equation for the reaction at the cathode when an object is silver plated.
model: Ag+ + e- → Ag.
exam.tip: Higher tier; reduction happens at the cathode.

exam.q: Give two reasons why metal objects are electroplated.
model: To improve appearance (e.g. shiny, attractive).
To improve resistance to corrosion.
exam.tip: These are the two spec reasons.

exam.q: Describe and explain the methods that can be used to prevent iron from rusting. Include examples of uses.
model: Rusting needs both oxygen and water, so excluding either prevents it.
Painting forms a barrier, e.g. cars, bridges; fails if chipped.
Oiling or greasing forms a barrier and lubricates, e.g. bike chains, machinery.
Plastic coating or tin plating form barriers, e.g. garden furniture, food cans.
Sacrificial protection: a more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium is attached, e.g. ship hulls, pipelines.
The more reactive metal is oxidised / loses electrons instead of iron, so protection works even if iron is exposed.
Galvanising (zinc coating) acts as both a barrier and sacrificial protection, e.g. roofs and buckets.
exam.tip: Organise your answer: why rusting happens, barrier methods, sacrificial methods, galvanising.

worked.q: A student set up three tubes: A (nail, tap water, open), B (nail, boiled water, oil layer, bung), C (nail, dry air with anhydrous calcium chloride, bung). After a week, only A had rusted. Write a conclusion.
steps: Compare A and B: only difference is oxygen. A rusted, B did not, so oxygen is needed.
Compare A and C: only difference is water. A rusted, C did not, so water is needed.
State the overall conclusion using both comparisons.
Mention a control: same type of nail, same time, same temperature.
worked.ans: Iron needs both oxygen and water to rust: removing oxygen (B) or water (C) prevents rusting.

worked.q: Model answer: explain how a steel spoon can be silver plated, including electrode equations.
steps: Clean the spoon so it is free of grease.
Connect the spoon to the negative terminal: it is the cathode.
Connect a bar of pure silver to the positive terminal: it is the anode.
Place both in an electrolyte of silver nitrate solution, which contains Ag+ ions.
Pass a direct current. At the cathode Ag+ ions are attracted, gain electrons and form silver: Ag+ + e- → Ag (reduction).
At the anode silver atoms lose electrons and dissolve: Ag → Ag+ + e- (oxidation), keeping the Ag+ concentration constant.
A longer time or larger current gives a thicker layer.
worked.ans: The spoon (cathode) becomes coated with silver from Ag+ ions in silver nitrate solution, supplied by a dissolving silver anode, improving appearance and corrosion resistance.

worked.q: Applied example: choose a rust prevention method for (a) a steel garden gate hinge, (b) a buried gas pipeline, (c) a corrugated steel roof. Justify each.
steps: (a) Hinge has moving parts, so paint would crack and rub off. Use oil or grease: barrier to oxygen and water, also lubricates.
(b) Pipeline is buried and cannot be repainted. Attach blocks of magnesium: more reactive than iron, oxidised instead of iron; replace blocks when used up.
(c) Roof is outdoors and may be scratched. Galvanise with zinc: barrier, plus sacrificial if scratched.
worked.ans: (a) oil/grease, (b) sacrificial magnesium blocks, (c) galvanising, each matched to how the object is used.

chem_edx.5.2.summary: An **alloy** is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually metals, or carbon in steel). The different-sized atoms **distort the regular layers** of the metal, so the layers **cannot slide over each other as easily**, making alloys **stronger and harder** than pure metals. Pure iron is too soft and iron straight from the blast furnace is too brittle, so iron is made into **steels** and **alloy steels** with useful properties such as corrosion resistance. Every metal or alloy is chosen because its **properties match its use**, for example aluminium and **magnalium** (low density), copper and **brass**, and gold.

core.p: A pure metal is a **giant lattice** of **positive metal ions** in **regular layers**, held together by **metallic bonding**: strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the **delocalised electrons**. Because all the atoms are the **same size**, the layers are flat and regular, so they can **slide over each other** when a force is applied, without the bonding breaking.
bullets: All atoms the **same size**, arranged in **regular layers**.
Layers can **slide over each other** easily, so pure metals are **soft**, **malleable** (can be hammered into shape) and **ductile** (can be drawn into wires).
The delocalised electrons move with the layers, so the metal bends rather than shattering.
Many pure metals (iron, aluminium, copper, gold) are **too soft** for jobs that need strength.

callouts.p: Can be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking.

core.p: An **alloy** is a **mixture** of a metal with one or more other elements, usually other metals (or carbon, in steel). Alloys keep many metallic properties (conduct electricity, shiny) but usually have **improved properties** such as greater strength, hardness or resistance to corrosion. Converting pure metals into alloys often **increases the strength** of the product.
bullets: Alloy = **mixture**, not a compound: the elements are not chemically bonded in fixed proportions.
Made by **melting** the metals together (or adding carbon to molten iron) and letting it solidify.
Properties can be **tailored** by changing which elements are added and how much.

Examples: **steel** (iron + carbon), **stainless steel** (iron + chromium + nickel), **brass** (copper + zinc), **magnalium** (aluminium + magnesium), jewellery **gold** (gold + copper/silver), bronze (copper + tin).

callouts.p: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually metals, which has improved properties compared with the pure metal.

core.h: Why alloys are stronger: the model
core.p: In an alloy the added atoms are a **different size** from the main metal atoms. They **distort (disrupt) the regular layers**, so the layers are no longer flat. This makes it **more difficult for the layers to slide over each other** when a force is applied. So the alloy is **harder and stronger** than the pure metal (and less malleable).
bullets: Step 1: pure metal has **identical atoms in regular layers**.
Step 2: alloy contains **atoms of different sizes**.
Step 3: these **distort the layers** of atoms.
Step 4: layers **cannot slide over each other as easily**.
Step 5: so the alloy is **harder / stronger** than the pure metal.
Mark schemes reward 'different sized atoms', 'distort the layers' and 'harder for layers to slide'.

callouts.p: Different sized atoms, distort the regular layers, so layers cannot slide over each other easily. Use all three for full marks.
Alloys are not stronger because the bonds are stronger. It is because the distorted layers cannot slide easily.

core.p: Iron from the **blast furnace** (cast iron) contains about 4% carbon and other impurities. It is **hard but brittle**, so it cracks easily and has limited uses. If all the carbon is removed, **pure iron** is too **soft** because its regular layers slide easily. So iron is converted into **steels** by controlling the carbon content and adding other metals, giving properties suited to each use.
bullets: **Cast iron** (blast furnace iron, about 4% carbon): hard, brittle; used for manhole covers, old cooking pans.
**Pure (wrought) iron**: soft and easily shaped; too soft for most structural uses.
**Steels**: iron with a controlled small amount of carbon; stronger and more useful.
**Alloy steels**: iron alloyed with **other metals** such as **chromium, nickel, manganese, tungsten, vanadium** to make them harder, stronger or more resistant to corrosion.
Iron is alloyed because pure iron is too soft and it **rusts easily**; alloying improves **strength, hardness and corrosion resistance**.

callouts.p: Iron is alloyed with other metals to produce alloy steels that are harder, stronger and/or more resistant to corrosion than pure iron.

core.p: Changing the **amount of carbon** and the **other metals** added gives steels with very different properties. More carbon makes steel harder and stronger but more brittle; chromium and nickel make it resistant to corrosion.
bullets: **Low carbon (mild) steel**: little carbon; **strong, malleable**, easily shaped; car bodies, wire, nails, girders.
**High carbon steel**: more carbon; **very hard and strong but brittle**; cutting tools, chisels, drill bits, saw blades.
**Stainless steel**: iron + **chromium** (and often **nickel**); **resistant to corrosion**, hard; cutlery, sinks, surgical instruments, saucepans.
Other alloy steels: **tungsten steel** stays hard at high temperatures (high-speed drill bits); **manganese steel** is very tough (rock crushers, rail points).

callouts.p: Car bodies need to be pressed into shape: low carbon steel (malleable). Knives and cutlery need to resist corrosion: stainless steel.

core.p: Spec point 5.7C asks you to explain how the **uses of metals are related to their properties** and the other way round. A good answer names the **property** and explains **why that property matters** for the use. Properties to think about: density, strength, hardness, malleability, ductility, electrical and thermal conductivity, reactivity (corrosion resistance), appearance and cost.
bullets: **Low density**: aircraft, bikes, car parts (less fuel needed).
**Good electrical conductor + ductile**: wires and cables.
**Unreactive / resists corrosion**: water pipes, jewellery, food cans, electrical contacts.
**Malleable**: car body panels, cans, foil.
**Hard and strong**: tools, girders, bearings.
**Attractive / lustrous**: jewellery, ornaments, decorative fittings.
Also consider **cost**: gold is excellent but too expensive for household wiring, so copper is used.

callouts.p: 'Copper is used for wires because it is a good conductor' scores one mark. Add 'and it is ductile so can be drawn into wires' for a second.

core.p: Aluminium is a reactive metal, but it is **protected by a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide** that forms on its surface, so it **resists corrosion**. It has a **low density** (about 2.7 g/cm3, about a third of iron's), is a **good conductor** of electricity and heat, and is **malleable**. Pure aluminium is quite **soft and weak**, so for strength it is used as **alloys**.
bullets: **Overhead power cables**: low density (light, so pylons can be further apart) and good conductor; wrapped around a **steel core** for strength.
**Drinks cans and foil**: malleable, low density, resists corrosion, non-toxic.
**Window frames, greenhouses**: resists corrosion, light.
**Aircraft**: low density, but used as alloys (e.g. with magnesium or copper) because pure aluminium is too weak.
Aluminium is not used for household wiring as much as copper because copper is the better conductor for thin wires.

callouts.p: Aluminium resists corrosion because of its protective oxide layer, not because it is unreactive.

core.p: **Magnalium** is an alloy of **aluminium and magnesium**. Typical engineering magnalium contains mostly aluminium with a few per cent magnesium. It is **stronger and harder than pure aluminium**, still has a **low density** (lighter than aluminium) and **resists corrosion**, which makes it ideal where both strength and lightness matter.
bullets: Composition: **aluminium + magnesium**.
Properties: **low density**, **stronger and harder** than pure aluminium, **corrosion resistant**.
Uses: **aircraft parts**, car parts, bike frames, some scientific instruments (e.g. telescope mirrors).
Why stronger: magnesium atoms are a **different size** from aluminium atoms, so they **distort the layers** and stop them sliding easily.
Alloys with a high proportion of magnesium (around 50%) are brittle and burn easily, so they are used in **fireworks** rather than structures.

callouts.p: Aluminium + magnesium: low density, strong, corrosion resistant; used in aircraft and car parts.

core.p: Copper is an **excellent conductor of electricity** (second only to silver), is **ductile** (can be drawn into wires) and **malleable**, and is **unreactive**: it does not react with water, so it does not corrode in pipes. Pure copper is quite soft.
bullets: **Electrical wiring**: very good conductor and ductile.
**Water pipes and hot water tanks**: does not react with water, malleable so pipes can be bent to shape, good thermal conductor.
**Saucepan bases**: good thermal conductor.
Gold would conduct and resist corrosion too, but is **far too expensive**; copper is a good compromise.

core.p: **Brass** is an alloy of **copper and zinc**. The zinc atoms are a different size from copper atoms, so brass is **harder and stronger than pure copper**. It **resists corrosion**, has an **attractive gold-like colour**, is easy to machine, and has **low friction**.
bullets: Composition: **copper + zinc**.
Properties: **harder than copper**, **resists corrosion**, attractive gold colour, conducts electricity, low friction.
**Musical instruments** (trumpets, trombones): easily shaped, attractive, resists corrosion.
**Door handles, knockers, taps, ornaments**: attractive and does not corrode.
**Electrical plug pins and connectors**: conducts electricity and is harder than copper, so it does not bend or wear.
Screws, hinges, gears: hard and low friction.

callouts.p: Use copper when maximum conductivity matters (wires); use brass when hardness matters too (plug pins).

core.p: Gold is **very unreactive**, so it **does not corrode or tarnish** and stays shiny. It is **malleable**, **ductile**, an excellent **conductor** and attractive. Pure gold is **very soft**, so jewellery is usually a **gold alloy** with copper or silver to make it **harder** and more hard-wearing. The purity of gold is measured in **carats**: pure gold is **24 carat**.
bullets: **Jewellery**: attractive, does not tarnish; alloyed with copper/silver so it does not scratch or bend easily.
**Electrical connectors** in computers and phones: excellent conductor that does not corrode, so contact stays reliable.
**Dental crowns/fillings**: unreactive, non-toxic, malleable.
Carats: **24 carat = 100% gold**, **18 carat = 18/24 = 75% gold**, **9 carat = 37.5% gold**.
Percentage of gold = (carats / 24) x 100.
Lower carat gold is **harder** but less valuable.

callouts.p: A measure of gold purity: the number of parts of gold out of 24. 24 carat is pure gold.

fig.cap: 18 carat gold is 18 parts gold out of 24 (75%); the other 25% is usually copper and/or silver, which makes the alloy harder than pure gold.

core.p: Expect: explain why alloys are stronger using a diagram or model (3 marks), explain why iron is made into steel, and choose or justify a metal for a use from data. Always tie each property to the job it does.
bullets: Use the words **different sized atoms**, **distort the layers**, **layers cannot slide easily**.
Draw alloy diagrams with **circles of a different size** among regular rows.
For uses, give **property + reason** (e.g. low density so the aircraft uses less fuel).
For data questions, quote numbers (density, conductivity, cost) and make a justified choice.
Remember the named alloys: **steel** (Fe + C), **stainless steel** (Fe + Cr + Ni), **brass** (Cu + Zn), **magnalium** (Al + Mg), gold alloys (Au + Cu/Ag).

callouts.p: Never call an alloy a compound. It is a mixture of a metal with other elements.

analogy.p: Imagine a tray of identical marbles in neat rows: tilt the tray and whole rows roll past each other easily, like the layers in a pure metal. Now drop a few golf balls in among the marbles: the rows are jumbled and jam against the bigger balls, so they cannot roll past each other easily, like the distorted layers in an alloy. Where it breaks down: marbles have nothing holding them together, whereas metal ions are held by strong metallic bonding with delocalised electrons, and in steel the carbon atoms are smaller than iron atoms, not larger.

terms.d: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually metals, with improved properties.
Electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.
Can be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking.
Can be drawn out into wires.
Breaks or shatters easily rather than bending.
Mass per unit volume; low density metals such as aluminium are light for their size.
Iron from the blast furnace, about 4% carbon; hard but brittle.
An alloy of iron with a small, controlled amount of carbon.
Steel with little carbon; strong and malleable, used for car bodies.
Steel with more carbon; very hard and strong but brittle, used for cutting tools.
Alloy steel of iron with chromium and nickel; resists corrosion, used for cutlery and sinks.
Iron alloyed with other metals (e.g. chromium, nickel, tungsten, manganese) to give special properties.
Alloy of aluminium and magnesium; low density, strong, corrosion resistant; used in aircraft parts.
Alloy of copper and zinc; harder than copper, corrosion resistant, used in musical instruments and plug pins.
Measure of gold purity, parts of gold out of 24; 24 carat is pure gold.
Ability of a metal not to be oxidised by oxygen and water in its surroundings.

mistakes.w: An alloy is a compound of two metals.
mistakes.r: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements.

mistakes.w: Alloys are stronger because the bonds between atoms are stronger.
mistakes.r: Different sized atoms distort the layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily.

mistakes.w: The layers in an alloy cannot move at all.
mistakes.r: The layers cannot slide over each other as easily; alloys can still be shaped with more force.

mistakes.w: Steel is a mixture of iron and other metals only.
mistakes.r: Steel is iron with carbon; alloy steels also contain other metals such as chromium and nickel.

mistakes.w: Stainless steel is used for cutlery because it is strong.
mistakes.r: Stainless steel is used for cutlery because it is resistant to corrosion (does not rust).

mistakes.w: Aluminium is used for aircraft because it is light.
mistakes.r: Aluminium (alloys) are used because they have a low density and are strong; 'light' alone may not score.

mistakes.w: Aluminium resists corrosion because it is unreactive.
mistakes.r: Aluminium is protected by a layer of aluminium oxide.

mistakes.w: Brass is made of copper and tin.
mistakes.r: Brass is copper and zinc (bronze is copper and tin).

mistakes.w: Pure gold is used for rings because it is hard.
mistakes.r: Pure gold is soft; it is alloyed with copper/silver to make it harder.

exam.q: What is meant by an alloy?
model: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually metals).
exam.tip: Must say mixture.

exam.q: Explain why alloys are harder than pure metals. You may use a diagram.
model: Alloys contain atoms of different sizes.
These distort the regular layers.
So the layers cannot slide over each other as easily.
exam.tip: A labelled diagram with different-sized circles can earn the marks.

exam.q: Explain why iron from the blast furnace is converted into steel.
model: Blast furnace iron contains about 4% carbon and is brittle.
Steel is stronger / less brittle / can be given properties for different uses.
exam.tip: Say what is wrong with the iron and what is better about steel.

exam.q: Give one reason why pure iron is not used for building bridges.
model: It is too soft (the layers slide easily) / it rusts easily.
exam.tip: Link back to the layer model if asked to explain.

exam.q: Stainless steel is used to make surgical instruments. Name two metals other than iron in stainless steel and give one property that makes it suitable.
model: Chromium.
Nickel.
Resistant to corrosion (does not rust) / hard.
exam.tip: Corrosion resistance is the key property.

exam.q: Explain why aluminium is used for overhead power cables.
model: Good conductor of electricity.
Low density, so the cable is light / fewer pylons needed (also resists corrosion).
exam.tip: Give two different properties with reasons.

exam.q: Magnalium is used to make aircraft parts. State what magnalium is made of and explain why it is suitable.
model: Aluminium and magnesium.
Low density, so less fuel needed.
Stronger than pure aluminium / resists corrosion.
exam.tip: Strength AND low density are both needed for aircraft.

exam.q: Brass is used to make the pins of electrical plugs. Explain why brass is used rather than pure copper.
model: Brass conducts electricity.
Brass is harder / stronger than copper, so the pins do not bend / wear.
exam.tip: Compare with copper.

exam.q: A ring is made of 18 carat gold. Calculate the percentage of gold in the ring and explain why pure gold is not used.
model: Pure gold is too soft.
Alloying with copper/silver makes it harder / scratch-resistant.
exam.tip: Show the working for the calculation mark.

exam.q: Explain why copper is used for household water pipes.
model: Copper does not react with water / does not corrode.
Malleable / easily bent into shape.
exam.tip: Any two relevant properties linked to pipes.

exam.q: Compare the uses of copper, aluminium and gold and explain how each use is related to the properties of the metal.
model: Copper: electrical wiring because it is an excellent conductor and ductile.
Copper: water pipes because it does not react with water and is malleable.
Aluminium: overhead cables and aircraft (as alloys) because of its low density.
Aluminium: cans and window frames because it resists corrosion due to its oxide layer.
Gold: jewellery because it is attractive and does not tarnish; alloyed to make it harder.
Gold: electrical connectors because it is an excellent conductor and does not corrode; too expensive for wiring.
exam.tip: For each metal give at least one use plus the property that explains it.

worked.q: Data: Metal P: density 2.7 g/cm3, good conductor, cost low. Metal Q: density 8.9 g/cm3, excellent conductor, cost medium. Metal R: density 19.3 g/cm3, excellent conductor, does not corrode, cost very high. Choose a metal for (a) overhead power cables and (b) household wiring. Justify.
steps: (a) Overhead cables hang between pylons, so low density matters most; they also need to conduct and be cheap over long distances.
P has the lowest density (2.7 g/cm3), conducts well and is cheap, so choose P (aluminium).
(b) Household wiring is thin and inside walls, so weight matters less; it must conduct very well.
Q is an excellent conductor at medium cost; R is too expensive.
So choose Q (copper).
worked.ans: (a) P (aluminium): low density and cheap; (b) Q (copper): excellent conductor at reasonable cost; R (gold) is too expensive.

worked.q: Calculate the mass of gold in a 9 carat gold chain of mass 12.0 g.
steps: 9 carat means 9 parts gold out of 24.
Fraction of gold = 9 / 24 = 0.375 (37.5%).
Mass of gold = 0.375 x 12.0 g.
worked.ans: 4.5 g of gold (the remaining 7.5 g is other metals such as copper and silver).

worked.q: Model answer: using a model, explain why brass is harder than pure copper.
steps: In pure copper all the atoms are the same size and are arranged in regular layers.
These layers can slide over each other easily when a force is applied, so copper is soft and malleable.
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc; zinc atoms are a different size from copper atoms.
The zinc atoms distort the regular layers of copper atoms.
This makes it more difficult for the layers to slide over each other.
So more force is needed to change the shape of brass: it is harder.
worked.ans: Different sized zinc atoms distort the copper layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily, making brass harder than copper.

chem_edx.5.3.summary: Concentration tells you how much solute is dissolved in each dm³ of solution, and it can be given either as a **mass per volume (g dm⁻³)** or as an **amount per volume (mol dm⁻³)**. The bridge between the two units is the **relative formula mass (Mr)**: multiply mol dm⁻³ by Mr to get g dm⁻³, and divide g dm⁻³ by Mr to get mol dm⁻³. Grade 9 answers convert volumes from cm³ to dm³ correctly, choose the right Mr from the formula, and show every step with units and sensible significant figures.

core.p: A solution is made when a **solute** dissolves in a **solvent**. Concentration measures how much solute is packed into a fixed volume of the solution. The fixed volume chemists use is **1 dm³** (one cubic decimetre, which is exactly 1 litre or 1000 cm³). The more solute in each dm³, the more concentrated the solution.
bullets: Concentration can be measured as **mass of solute per dm³** (unit g dm⁻³).
Concentration can also be measured as **amount of solute in moles per dm³** (unit mol dm⁻³).
Both describe the same solution; they just count the solute differently (by grams or by particles).
The volume is always the volume of the **solution**, not the volume of water added.
A more concentrated solution has more solute particles in the same volume, so it has a larger value in either unit.

callouts.p: The amount (or mass) of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution, usually 1 dm³.

core.p: This is the core (all students) way of describing concentration. You find it by dividing the mass of solute in grams by the volume of solution in dm³. It is easy to measure in the lab because you can weigh a solid on a balance.
bullets: **concentration (g dm⁻³) = mass of solute (g) ÷ volume of solution (dm³)**
Rearranged: **mass (g) = concentration (g dm⁻³) × volume (dm³)**
Example: 10 g of sodium chloride dissolved to make 0.500 dm³ of solution has concentration 10 ÷ 0.500 = 20 g dm⁻³.
g dm⁻³ does not tell you how many particles are present, because different substances have different masses per particle.

callouts.p: concentration in g dm⁻³ = mass of solute in g ÷ volume of solution in dm³

core.p: Chemists usually prefer mol dm⁻³ because reactions happen between particles, and the mole counts particles. Two solutions with the same mol dm⁻³ contain the same number of solute formula units per dm³, even if the substances have very different masses.
bullets: **concentration (mol dm⁻³) = amount of solute (mol) ÷ volume of solution (dm³)**
Rearranged: **amount (mol) = concentration (mol dm⁻³) × volume (dm³)**
The amount in moles is found from mass using **moles = mass (g) ÷ Mr**.
mol dm⁻³ is the unit used in titration calculations and balanced-equation ratios.
A solution of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ is sometimes written as 1.0 M in older books, but write mol dm⁻³ in the exam.

callouts.p: concentration in mol dm⁻³ = amount of solute in mol ÷ volume of solution in dm³

core.h: Why Mr is the link between the two units
core.p: The relative formula mass Mr tells you the mass in grams of **one mole** of a substance. So if you know how many moles are in each dm³, multiplying by the mass of one mole gives the mass in each dm³. Going the other way, dividing the mass in each dm³ by the mass of one mole tells you how many moles there are in each dm³. The volume (1 dm³) stays the same in both, so only the top line changes.
bullets: **g dm⁻³ = mol dm⁻³ × Mr**
**mol dm⁻³ = g dm⁻³ ÷ Mr**
This is exactly the same as **mass = moles × Mr**, just applied to one dm³ of solution.
Mr has **no units** (it is a relative mass), but the mass of one mole has units g mol⁻¹, which is why the units work out.
Unit check: mol dm⁻³ × g mol⁻¹ = g dm⁻³ (the mol cancels).

callouts.p: Grams are bigger numbers than moles for any substance with Mr above 1, so going to g dm⁻³ you multiply (number gets bigger) and going to mol dm⁻³ you divide (number gets smaller).

core.p: Every conversion needs the correct Mr. Add up the relative atomic masses (Ar) of every atom in the formula, remembering to multiply out brackets and subscripts. Use the Ar values given on the periodic table in the exam.
bullets: A wrong Mr loses the conversion mark even if the method is perfect, so double check brackets.

core.p: Lab volumes are measured in cm³ (burettes, pipettes and measuring cylinders), but concentration units use dm³. A cube 10 cm on each side has a volume of 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³, and that same cube is 1 dm on each side, so 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.
bullets: **cm³ to dm³: divide by 1000** (for example 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³).
**dm³ to cm³: multiply by 1000** (for example 0.150 dm³ = 150 cm³).
Forgetting to convert is the single most common reason for losing marks: answers come out 1000 times too small.
Volume conversions are needed when calculating concentration from a mass and volume; they are not needed when simply converting g dm⁻³ to mol dm⁻³ because both are already per dm³.

callouts.p: If a question only asks you to change 0.25 mol dm⁻³ into g dm⁻³, there is no volume to convert: just multiply by Mr.

core.h: Method: mol dm⁻³ to g dm⁻³
core.p: Use this when you know the molar concentration and want the mass concentration, for example to work out what mass of solid to weigh out for every dm³ of solution.
bullets: Step 1: write the formula and calculate Mr.
Step 2: **multiply** the concentration in mol dm⁻³ by Mr.
Step 3: give the answer with the unit **g dm⁻³** and a sensible number of significant figures.
Example: 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH → 0.100 × 40 = **4.00 g dm⁻³**.

core.h: Method: g dm⁻³ to mol dm⁻³
core.p: Use this when a solution is labelled with a mass concentration but you need moles, for example in a titration or reacting-ratio question.
bullets: Step 1: write the formula and calculate Mr.
Step 2: **divide** the concentration in g dm⁻³ by Mr.
Step 3: give the answer with the unit **mol dm⁻³**.
Example: 14.6 g dm⁻³ HCl → 14.6 ÷ 36.5 = **0.400 mol dm⁻³**.
Check: 0.400 × 36.5 = 14.6, so the answer reverses correctly.

core.h: Starting from a mass and a volume
core.p: Many exam questions give you a mass of solid dissolved in a volume in cm³ and ask for the concentration in mol dm⁻³. There are two equally valid routes, and both must give the same answer. Choose one and lay it out clearly.
bullets: **Route A (via moles):** moles = mass ÷ Mr, then concentration = moles ÷ volume in dm³.
**Route B (via g dm⁻³):** concentration = mass ÷ volume in dm³ to get g dm⁻³, then divide by Mr.
Example: 2.00 g NaOH made up to 250 cm³. Route A: 2.00 ÷ 40 = 0.0500 mol; 0.0500 ÷ 0.250 = 0.200 mol dm⁻³.
Route B: 2.00 ÷ 0.250 = 8.00 g dm⁻³; 8.00 ÷ 40 = 0.200 mol dm⁻³ (same answer).
Working backwards: mass needed = concentration (mol dm⁻³) × volume (dm³) × Mr.

callouts.p: Most marks are for method. Write each formula, substitute numbers with units, then give the answer. A correct final answer with no working may still gain full marks, but a wrong one with no working gets nothing.

core.h: Linking to titrations and reacting amounts
core.p: This conversion is the final step in many titration questions: you work out the concentration of an unknown solution in mol dm⁻³ from the titration results, and the question then asks for the concentration in g dm⁻³. It also lets you compare solutions that are labelled in different units.
bullets: Titration answers come out in mol dm⁻³ because they use mole ratios from the balanced equation.
To give the answer in g dm⁻³, multiply by the Mr of **the substance whose concentration is asked**, not the other reactant.
To compare two solutions fairly, convert both into mol dm⁻³: equal mol dm⁻³ means equal numbers of solute particles per dm³.
Diluting a solution does not change the moles of solute, only the volume, so concentration in both units falls by the same factor.

callouts.p: Always use the Mr of the solute in the solution you are describing.

core.p: Edexcel mark schemes usually accept answers to 2 or 3 significant figures if the data are given to that precision, but they penalise missing or wrong units when the unit is asked for. Keep full calculator values during the working and round only at the end.
bullets: Give the answer to the same number of significant figures as the least precise data (usually 3).
Do not round intermediate values such as moles too early; rounding 0.04545 to 0.05 can change the final answer.
Write the unit as **g dm⁻³** or **mol dm⁻³**; 'g/dm³' and 'mol/dm³' are also accepted.
Never write 'g' alone or 'mol' alone for a concentration: that is a mass or an amount, not a concentration.

callouts.p: dm³ is a volume; dm⁻³ means 'per dm³'. A concentration unit always has dm⁻³ (per volume) in it.

analogy.p: Imagine jars of sweets, each jar 1 dm³. You can describe how full a jar is by the **total mass of sweets** in it (like g dm⁻³) or by the **number of bags of sweets** (like mol dm⁻³, where one 'bag' is a mole). If you know how heavy one bag is (the Mr), you multiply bags by bag mass to get total mass, or divide total mass by bag mass to get the number of bags. Two jars with the same number of bags can have very different masses if one brand of sweet is heavier. Where it breaks down: a mole is a fixed number of particles (6.02 × 10²³), not a bag you can pick a size for, and dissolved particles are spread evenly through the solution rather than sitting in clumps.

terms.d: The substance that dissolves in a solvent to form a solution.
The liquid in which a solute dissolves, often water.
A mixture formed when a solute dissolves in a solvent.
The amount or mass of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution, usually 1 dm³.
Unit of mass concentration: grams of solute per cubic decimetre of solution.
Unit of molar concentration: moles of solute per cubic decimetre of solution.
Cubic decimetre, a volume equal to 1000 cm³ or 1 litre.
Cubic centimetre, a volume equal to 1 ml; 1000 cm³ = 1 dm³.
The amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles (the Avogadro constant).
The average mass of an atom of an element compared with one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula of a substance.
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams, numerically equal to its Mr (unit g mol⁻¹).
The quantity of a substance measured in moles; moles = mass ÷ Mr.
A solution whose concentration is accurately known.
Adding more solvent so the same amount of solute is spread through a larger volume, lowering concentration.

mistakes.w: Dividing g dm⁻³ by Mr gives g dm⁻³.
mistakes.r: Dividing g dm⁻³ by Mr gives **mol dm⁻³**; multiplying mol dm⁻³ by Mr gives g dm⁻³.

mistakes.w: Multiplying by Mr to go from g dm⁻³ to mol dm⁻³.
mistakes.r: To go from g dm⁻³ to mol dm⁻³ you must **divide** by Mr.

mistakes.w: Using the volume in cm³ directly, e.g. 0.05 mol ÷ 250 = 0.0002 mol dm⁻³.
mistakes.r: Convert to dm³ first: 250 cm³ = 0.250 dm³, so 0.05 ÷ 0.250 = **0.20 mol dm⁻³**.

mistakes.w: Mr of H₂SO₄ = 1 + 32 + 16 = 49.
mistakes.r: Multiply by the subscripts: (2 × 1) + 32 + (4 × 16) = **98**.
The bracket doubles both O and H: 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = **74**.

mistakes.w: Using the Mr of the other reactant from the titration when converting to g dm⁻³.
mistakes.r: Use the Mr of **the solute whose concentration is being asked for**.

mistakes.w: Giving the unit as 'g' or 'mol' for a concentration.
mistakes.r: A concentration unit must be **per volume**: g dm⁻³ or mol dm⁻³.

mistakes.w: Dividing the volume by 1000 again when changing 0.20 mol dm⁻³ to g dm⁻³.
mistakes.r: Both units are already per dm³, so **just multiply by Mr**; no volume conversion is needed.

mistakes.w: Rounding moles to 1 significant figure halfway through.
mistakes.r: Keep full values in the calculator and **round only the final answer**, usually to 3 significant figures.

exam.q: State the unit of concentration used when the amount of solute is measured in moles.
model: mol dm⁻³ (allow mol/dm³)
exam.tip: Always include 'per volume' in a concentration unit.

exam.q: Convert 250 cm³ into dm³.
model: 0.250 dm³ (allow 0.25)
exam.tip: Divide cm³ by 1000 to get dm³.

exam.q: A solution of sodium hydroxide, NaOH, has a concentration of 0.500 mol dm⁻³. Calculate its concentration in g dm⁻³. (Relative atomic masses: H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23)
exam.tip: Moles to grams: multiply by Mr.

exam.q: A bottle of hydrochloric acid has a concentration of 7.30 g dm⁻³. Calculate the concentration in mol dm⁻³. (H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
model: Mr HCl = 36.5
exam.tip: Grams to moles: divide by Mr.

exam.q: Calculate the relative formula mass of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, and hence the mass concentration of a 0.150 mol dm⁻³ solution. (H = 1, O = 16, S = 32)
exam.tip: Multiply each Ar by its subscript before adding.

exam.q: 4.00 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in water and made up to 500 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in g dm⁻³.
exam.tip: This is the core g dm⁻³ formula: mass ÷ volume in dm³.

exam.q: 5.30 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, is dissolved and made up to 250 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration of the solution in mol dm⁻³. (C = 12, O = 16, Na = 23)
model: concentration = 0.0500 ÷ 0.250 = 0.200 mol dm⁻³
exam.tip: Set out each step on its own line so each method mark is clear.

exam.q: A student needs 200 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ potassium hydroxide, KOH, solution. Calculate the mass of KOH they must weigh out. (H = 1, O = 16, K = 39)
exam.tip: Work backwards: moles = concentration × volume, then mass = moles × Mr.

exam.q: Solution X is sodium chloride at 11.7 g dm⁻³. Solution Y is sodium hydroxide at 8.0 g dm⁻³. Show which solution contains more moles of solute per dm³. (NaCl Mr = 58.5, NaOH Mr = 40)
model: they contain the same number of moles per dm³ (equal concentration in mol dm⁻³)
exam.tip: To compare particle numbers, compare mol dm⁻³, not g dm⁻³.

exam.q: From a titration, the concentration of a sulfuric acid solution was found to be 0.0750 mol dm⁻³. Calculate its concentration in g dm⁻³ and explain why chemists often prefer mol dm⁻³.
model: Mr H₂SO₄ = 98
mol dm⁻³ tells you the number of particles (moles) per dm³
reactions take place in mole ratios given by the balanced equation, so mol dm⁻³ can be used directly in calculations
exam.tip: Explain marks need the idea that reactions depend on particle numbers, not masses.

worked.q: Convert 0.200 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, into g dm⁻³. (H = 1, O = 16, S = 32)
steps: We are going from moles to grams, so multiply by Mr.
0.200 mol dm⁻³ × 98 = 19.6 g dm⁻³
worked.ans: 19.6 g dm⁻³

worked.q: A solution contains 2.92 g of hydrogen chloride, HCl, in 400 cm³. Calculate the concentration in g dm⁻³ and in mol dm⁻³. (H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
steps: Volume in dm³ = 400 ÷ 1000 = 0.400 dm³
Concentration = mass ÷ volume = 2.92 ÷ 0.400 = 7.30 g dm⁻³
Concentration in mol dm⁻³ = 7.30 ÷ 36.5 = 0.200 mol dm⁻³
Check by the other route: moles = 2.92 ÷ 36.5 = 0.0800 mol; 0.0800 ÷ 0.400 = 0.200 mol dm⁻³
worked.ans: 7.30 g dm⁻³ and 0.200 mol dm⁻³

worked.q: What mass of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, is needed to make 250 cm³ of a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution? (C = 12, O = 16, Na = 23)
steps: Moles needed = concentration × volume = 0.100 × 0.250 = 0.0250 mol
Mass = moles × Mr = 0.0250 × 106 = 2.65 g
Alternative: 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × 106 = 10.6 g dm⁻³; 10.6 × 0.250 = 2.65 g
